name: Pearl Copper
lede: Pearl Copper is a reddish brown taken from RAL 8029, the German industrial color standard, named for the sheen of metallic copper.

sections.title: An industrial swatch, not a pigment
sections.body:
Our library lists Pearl Copper as RAL 8029, an entry in the RAL standard, Germany's system of numbered colors for paint and industrial coatings [1]. RAL began in 1927 as a committee project, Reichs-Ausschuß für Lieferbedingungen, which issued a first set of forty swatches, RAL 840, so that factories and customers could order a color by number instead of trading physical samples [2]. The system has grown steadily since, and 8029 is one of its later "pearl" finishes, named for an actual metallic-flake coating rather than any dye or pigment [1][2].

The nearest named colors on file are [[mahogany-red]] and [[morocco-red]], at Beyond the RAL code, no further naming history is documented here [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A screen match for this brown turns up in 2,172 of 23,781 paintings, about 9.1 percent, as photographed, among the more common tones in the archive [1]. Its rate rises sharply before 1600, when it covers nearly a fifth of paintings from the 1400s, then falls steadily into the twentieth century [1]. Painters working in Spanish and Venetian portraiture, such as Juan de Juanes and Paolo Veronese, carry it well above the archive's average [1]. The figure is a computed color match on aged, varnished paintings, not a claim about any pigment used [1].

questions.q: Pearl Copper comes from which numbering system?
True or false: another name in our library, Copper Brown, shares the exact same hex value as Pearl Copper.

openers: Pearl Copper shares its exact hex value with another library name, Copper Brown — two names, one color.

issues: No concordance hits; RAL founding history from one web source (Wikipedia), hedged. No further documentation found for the specific 8029 naming.
